titles.text: The little man with the scorched legs

description.en: R. Zera was a student of R. Yehudah b. Yehezkel in Babylonia. Yet he greatly yearned to move to the Land of Israel and fasted for 100 days before he could feel worthy to do so. There, he studied under R. Elazar b. Pedat and R. Abahu and became known as the Pious Man of Babylonia.
description.he: רבי זירא היה תלמידו של רבי יהודה בר יחזקאל בבבל. הוא השתוקק לעלות לארץ ישראל והתענה מאה תעניות כדי שיהיה ראוי לכך. כשעלה ארצה, למד עם רבי אלעזר בן פדת ועם רבי אבהו והיה מוכר כאחד מ"חסידי בבל".

en.title: Rabbi Zeira's Title
en.prompt: The Talmud occasionally refers to Rav Zeira instead of Rabbi Zeira, and in tractate Ketubot, it gives two alternative attributions for one teaching, one to Rav Zeira and one to Rabbi Zeira. Rashi explains his opinion that these are in fact the same person, and the disagreement between the attributions is whether he gave this teaching before or after he had been ordained as a 'Rabbi' in the land of Israel.

en.title: The Gentle Scholars of Jerusalem
en.prompt: The scholars in Jerusalem were renowned for their harmonious and non-contentious demeanor, a sharp contrast to the more disputatious scholars of Babylonia. Rav Zera's example, as depicted in the 16th-century work Netivot Olam by the Maharal of Prague, further illustrates this distinction between the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds, emphasizing the contrasting approaches of scholars in these regions.
en.ai_prompt: The scholars in Jerusalem were known for their pleasant and non-disputatious nature, in contrast to the more contentious scholars in Babylonia. en.title: The Primacy of Study Over Debate
en.ai_title: The Primacy of Study Over Debate
en.prompt: The path to spiritual growth and atonement, as articulated in Orchot Tzadikim, emphasizes the supremacy of Torah study and personal improvement over contentious debates. This ethical work cites Rabbi Zera's example from Bava Metzia, where he undertook a hundred-day fast to distance himself from Babylonian teachings, underscoring the importance of dedicated study in achieving spiritual clarity and virtue.
en.ai_prompt: The key to spiritual growth and atonement lies in increasing one's study and repetition of the Talmud, rather than engaging in intense argumentative discourse. The 15th-century ethical work Orchot Tzadikim emphasizes the importance of Torah study and self-improvement over sharp debate.

en.title: The Piety of Rabbi Zera
en.prompt: Rabbi Zera's intense personal piety and self-discipline are exemplified by his numerous fasts and his practice of testing himself with a heated oven to ensure his spiritual purity. The Ein Yaakov, a 16th-century compilation of Talmudic stories and parables, offers a glimpse into the deep spiritual and ascetic practices of the sages.
